definition: The Automated Similarity Judgment Program (ASJP) is a collaborative project applying computational approaches to comparative linguistics using a database of word lists.
details: The database is open access and consists of 40-item basic-vocabulary lists for well over half of the world's languages. It is continuously being expanded. In addition to isolates and languages of demonstrated genealogical groups, the database includes pidgins, creoles, mixed languages, and constructed languages. Words of the database are transcribed into a simplified standard orthography (ASJPcode). The database has been used to estimate dates at which language families have diverged into daughter languages by a method related to but still different from glottochronology, to determine the homeland (Urheimat) of a proto-language, to investigate sound symbolism, to evaluate different phylogenetic methods, and several other purposes. ASJP is not widely accepted among historical linguists as an adequate method to establish or evaluate relationships between language families. It is part of the Cross-Linguistic Linked Data project hosted by the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History.

explainer.lead: The Automated Similarity Judgment Program (ASJP) uses standardized word lists to compare languages computationally. Its broad, open-access database makes large-scale language comparisons possible, although its approach to establishing language-family relationships is not widely accepted by historical linguists.

tiers.eli5: Imagine giving many languages the same short list of everyday words, then writing those words in a shared alphabet so a computer can compare them. ASJP does this with 40-word lists, helping researchers look for patterns across a huge number of languages. The comparisons can suggest connections, but they do not settle disagreements about how languages are related.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers use ASJP by transcribing words from 40-item basic-vocabulary lists into ASJPcode and analyzing the standardized lists computationally. Applications include divergence-date and homeland estimation, sound-symbolism studies, and evaluation of phylogenetic methods. Treat inferred genealogical relationships cautiously because ASJP is not widely accepted among historical linguists as an adequate way to establish or evaluate them.
tiers.paperLevel: ASJP is a collaborative comparative-linguistics project built on an open-access database of 40-item basic-vocabulary lists, with lexical items normalized into ASJPcode for computational comparison. Its coverage extends beyond isolates and established genealogical groups to pidgins, creoles, mixed languages, and constructed languages. A principal limitation is its lack of broad acceptance among historical linguists as an adequate method for establishing or evaluating language-family relationships.

explainer.example: A researcher could transcribe the same 40 basic meanings from several languages into ASJPcode, compare the resulting lists computationally, and use the analysis to help evaluate different proposed language family trees.

usedIn.name: Language divergence dating

usedIn.detail: Comparing and assessing different computational methods for inferring language histories.

explainer.intuition: Languages become easier to compare at scale when equivalent basic vocabulary is written in one simplified transcription system. ASJP turns that idea into a shared database and a basis for computational analysis.
howItWorks: Collect a 40-item basic-vocabulary list for each language.
Transcribe the words into the simplified ASJPcode orthography.
Store the standardized lists in the open-access ASJP database.
Compare lists computationally and apply the results to linguistic questions.
explainer.whyItMatters: ASJP provides word lists for well over half of the world's languages and continues to expand, enabling comparisons that would be difficult to assemble individually. Its open database supports several kinds of cross-linguistic research while also prompting debate about computational judgments of language relatedness.
misconceptions: ASJP comparisons are not broadly accepted proof of language-family relationships.
The database is not limited to isolates and established families; it also includes pidgins, creoles, mixed languages, and constructed languages.
Its divergence-dating method is related to glottochronology but is not identical to it.
